newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan warms to greater world role for yen.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan warms to greater world role for yen.

text.p: Japan, once wary of global yen holding due to concerns it might lose control over its exchange rate and liquidity, is moving towards a greater international role for the currency.
As a result it is looking at regional arrangements with central banks in the Asia-Pacific region to improve the yen's liquidity, similar to a system already in place for the dollar.
Takashi Anzai, executive director of the Bank of Japan (BOJ), told Reuters, "We are considering yen repo arrangements to ensure the liquidity of the yen in the region."
The BOJ controls liquidity of the yen, and the yen repo scheme would give Asian central banks instant access to emergency yen liquidity without the knowledge of the market, Anzai said.
This boosts liquidity of the yen while reducing the risks in holding the currency, he said.
The scheme enables Asian central banks to raise yen-based cash in times of liquidity squeeze using yen-denominated short-term debt in their reserves as collateral for yen loans from the BOJ.

"This can be considered a first step toward the expanded use of the yen and eventually the future establishment of an Asian currency basket similar to the EU," said Teruhiko Mano, adviser to the president of the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
Under this system, the region has an alternative reserve currency to the U.S. dollar, he said.

In a landmark step in Asia-Pacific regional cooperation, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) and the BOJ entered into a U.S. dollar-based repurchase agreement with seven Asia-Pacific central banks on April 25.
Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, has said he is considering a way of using yen-denominated assets to stabilise the currency market.

C.H. Kwan, senior economist at Nomura Research Institute Ltd's Center for Policy Research said, "The yen repo scheme shows that Japanese bureaucrats are eager to promote the use of the yen as an international currency."
"However, the BOJ, and the Ministry of Finance (MOF) may have different objectives in mind," Kwan said.

"The central bank is geared to the creation of a fully-fledged, deregulated money market that ensures easier access to the yen by foreigners, while the MOF appears more concerned about the stability of the yen," he said.
The BOJ's Anzai said there were critical hurdles to overcome in bringing the yen on to the global stage.

"The real obstacles to the liquidity of the yen, which are restricting its use and holding by the global financial community, are an illiquid short-term government debt market and taxation and other regulations surrounding it," Anzai said.
Central banks' substantial holding of yen reserves are a prerequisite for the yen repo arrangements.

Foreign reserves in Asia already exceed those of the Group of Seven industrialised economies and account for 40 percent of world reserves. However, the yen's proportion remains low compared with that of the U.S. dollar.
"The urgent task is the establishment of highly transparent financial and capital markets that are easy for overseas yen holders to use," Mano said.
This means enacting structural reforms that inevitably will entail some pain, he said.

It is widely known among Japanese banks that the ministry is reluctant to fully liberalise the short-term debt market as it means giving up the current taxation and legal framework through which the ministry exercises its power, bankers said.
The drastic overhaul of the money market also means more authority of the BOJ in managing policies, they said.
BOJ'S INDEPENDENCE
Japan is moving to revise a wartime statute governing the BOJ and make the central bank more independent from the Finance Ministry.
The government plans to present a bill to revise the BOJ Law for debate in the next ordinary session of the Diet that starts in January.
This involves making the Bank more involved in the decision making process in international monetary affairs, including the yen repo arrangements.
FOREX IMPLICATION
A yen repo pact, though it may add to the yen's stability, may have strategic implications for the Bank beyond the currency market stability.
Yen cash raised via the repo pact can be used as intervention resources in the foreign exchange markets.
But, the pact itself does not necessarily point to a stronger or weaker yen, the Bank's Anzai said.
The United States wants to be part of the process of increased economic and currency cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region, but has not shown any desire to become involved in the arrangements.
REGIONAL EFFORT
The Bank of Japan is already furthering regional central bank ties through EMEAP (Executive Meeting of East Asia and Pacific Central Banks), an 11 member group set up on the BOJ's initiative in 1991.
This could promote structural changes in Japan's financial markets as well as a more strategic goal of boosting the regional profile of the yen, analysts said.
"It is apparent that the Asian region is underdeveloped in terms of markets, settlement, banking system and the central banks' role in the financial sector," Anzai said.

In order to maintain sustainable growth, a stable financial system and mature market mechanism are indispensible because the traditional flow of aid and direct investment alone can no longer support the region's growth, Anzai said.
"It is necessary that EMEAP provide incentives to enhance mutual understanding and to improve the system to match global standards," he said.
EMEAP groups central banks of Australia, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, South Korea and New Zealand.
